account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts poaching risk and plans patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Rangers received center coordinates of fifteen 3 x 3 km blocks chosen from PAWS risk predictions, without being told each block's risk class. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran from February to March 2019. In that trial, high-risk blocks yielded 7 detections in 22 cells, and low-risk blocks yielded 0 detections in 34 cells. The developers and staff of the operating organizations reported both trials in a peer-reviewed paper published in 2020. On 5 November 2020, Mongabay reported that PAWS had been incorporated into the SMART conservation software, which rangers use in parks around the world. Mongabay also reported that Srepok rangers had reported finding 5 to 20 times more snares since they started using PAWS.

ai_role.statement: The AI's output (risk-ranked 3 x 3 km blocks) determined where patrols went. Rangers were blinded to risk class. High-risk blocks yielded detections while low-risk blocks yielded none. The paper itself cautions that the first QENP test's increased findings “may be partially explained by factors beyond the predictive model”. The 1,000-versus-200–300 comparison relies on rangers' reported averages, not a controlled baseline. The peer-reviewed paper is written by the system's academic developers together with staff of the operating organizations (WWF, WCS, Uganda Wildlife Authority). There is no commercial vendor.

fields.account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts poaching risk and plans patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Rangers received center coordinates of fifteen 3 x 3 km blocks chosen from PAWS risk predictions, without being told each block's risk class. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran from February to March 2019. In that trial, high-risk blocks yielded 7 detections in 22 cells, and low-risk blocks yielded 0 detections in 34 cells. The developers and staff of the operating organizations reported both trials in a peer-reviewed paper published in 2020. On 5 November 2020, Mongabay reported that PAWS had been incorporated into the SMART conservation software, which rangers use in parks around the world. Mongabay also reported that Srepok rangers had reported finding 5 to 20 times more snares since they started using PAWS.

purpose: PAWS was built to predict where poaching will occur and to prescribe patrol routes that maximize the detection and removal of snares. The snare removals are this intended benefit.

ratings.reason: The ranger force's monthly snare removals rose from a reported two or three hundred to over one thousand. A chi-squared test confirmed that the predictions discriminated risk (p = 0.023).

Over one thousand snares were removed from a sanctuary that is identified as a site for reintroducing tigers. The paper states that each snare “represents the life of one animal potentially saved”. No source documents a change in an animal population.
